title: Texas Lawmaker Revives Mexico Guest-Worker Plan as H-1B Scrutiny Grows
excerpt: Rep. Josey Garcia's HB 294 would have Texas seek federal permission to coordinate temporary Mexican workers for short-staffed employers — a revival of a bill the House rejected 65–76 in 2025, with no change to H-1B itself.
body:
• State Rep. Josey Garcia, a Democrat, filed House Bill 294 on Monday, November 9, proposing a state-coordinated programme to bring temporary workers from Mexico to Texas businesses.
  • The bill creates no new visa. Texas would first need federal authorisation, and workers would enter on existing federal nonimmigrant visas for jobs the Texas Workforce Commission identifies as short-staffed.
  • HB 294 does not change H-1B rules and gives Indian professionals no new route or new restriction — it is a separate channel aimed mainly at temporary skilled and unskilled jobs outside the H-1B system.
  • A near-identical bill, HB 2858, failed in the Texas House in May 2025 by 65 votes to 76, so this is a second attempt, not a new idea.

A Texas Democrat has revived a plan for the state to help employers recruit temporary workers from Mexico, filing the proposal on Monday, November 9, even as state and federal officials tighten scrutiny of foreign-worker programmes including H-1B. State Rep. Josey Garcia of District 124 filed House Bill 294, which would instruct the governor to seek federal permission before Texas pursues any agreement with a Mexican state, according to The Dallas Express.

What HB 294 Would Actually Do

The bill would not create a new visa category or authorise anyone to work in Texas without federal approval. Instead, Texas would coordinate recruitment through existing federal nonimmigrant visas, for skilled and unskilled positions that the Texas Workforce Commission identifies as needing workers. The mechanism matters: immigration and visas remain federal, so the state programme could operate only after Washington grants authorisation, and only inside visa categories Congress has already created.

Employers who took part would have to demonstrate that sufficient able, willing, qualified and available workers cannot fill the jobs in the relevant labour market. They would also have to certify that hiring temporary guest workers would not harm the wages or working conditions of similarly employed Texas workers.

The participating Mexican state, in turn, would have to supply workers who meet federal visa requirements, pass criminal background checks and undergo standardised education or skills testing. Workers would receive tamper-proof identification carrying their personal information, photograph, fingerprint, visa number and visa expiration date. Mexican officials would notify the employer, the governor and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement if a worker failed to return to Mexico before the visa expired.

The Safeguards Stop Short of an Enforcement System

The bill does not specify a new Texas audit system, a public employer registry or a state penalty for an inaccurate labour-shortage certification, and it does not appropriate a specific amount of money to administer the programme. Those omissions leave open the questions lawmakers are likely to press as the bill moves: which occupations face documented shortages, who checks employer certifications, what oversight taxpayers would fund, and how investigators would detect false statements or visa abuse.

A Second Attempt After a 2025 Defeat

The proposal revives a concept the House rejected last session. House Bill 2858, authored by State Reps. Ray Lopez, a Democrat from District 125, and Drew Darby, a Republican from District 72, with Garcia and Suleman Lalani, a Democrat from District 76, as co-authors, failed in the House by 65 votes to 76 on May 12, 2025. The earlier bill's bipartisan sponsorship means the guest-worker idea does not belong exclusively to Democrats. Its official bill analysis argued that labour shortages have defined this decade, that Texas still had more open positions than unemployed workers, and that the state should seek a federal waiver so the governor could negotiate a memorandum of understanding with a Mexican state. The full text of HB 2858 set out the same framework Garcia's bill now repeats.

The H-1B Backdrop

The guest-worker proposal reaches beyond H-1B. H-1B generally covers specialty occupations, while H-2A and H-2B cover qualifying temporary agricultural and non-agricultural jobs — the categories a Mexico programme would most plausibly use. The filing lands in a state actively debating foreign labour: Texas ranked second nationally with 109,130 positions in certified H-1B, H-1B1 and E-3 labour condition applications during the first nine months of fiscal 2026, according to figures The Dallas Express has previously documented. Those certifications do not equal visas issued or people actually employed.

On the restriction side, Gov. Greg Abbott's January 27 directive limited new H-1B petitions by certain state agencies and public universities through May 31, 2027, unless the Texas Workforce Commission grants written permission. Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller has separately moved to restrict certain state grants to businesses employing H-1B workers — a step we covered in our report on the Agriculture Department's grant rules. At the federal level, regulators are considering a proposal to end the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days for certain foreign workers who lose their jobs; comments close November 10 and the proposal has not taken effect, as we reported in our explainer on the grace-period proposal.

What Happens Next — and What Readers Should Do

For now, nothing changes for any worker or employer. HB 294 has only been filed; it is not law, and no application exists to file. If lawmakers enact it, the governor would have to seek federal authorisation promptly and could then choose whether to negotiate a memorandum of understanding with a Mexican state. The measure would take effect immediately if it passes each chamber by two-thirds, or on September 1, 2027, without that supermajority. Indian professionals on H-1B visas should read this bill as context, not as a change to their status: their rules continue to be set by federal agencies and courts, and the practical step is simply to watch whether HB 294 clears committee in the coming session.
